So here's the thing... There's a difference between living in space and camping there. A difference between 'settlements' and 'outposts'. Manned outposts in space don't really have a future. We're moving out of the flag-planting heroic era of space. There really isn't anything practical we need humans physically in space to do anymore. Our future in space looks like this. Our last practical job in space is to be a solution to telecommunications latency--and even that might only be for another 30 years.

So the idea that going to space is about 'roughing it' is erroneous. We don't need to 'rough it'. We don't strictly need to go to space ourselves anymore to do those things we've assumed require us to 'rough it' because machines are doing all the heavy lifting out there. And that's a good thing because we can't all be astronauts. We can't rely on a handful of elites to get stuff done out there anymore than we can rely on Olympic athletes to build our houses. If we go to space we go there to live, not for the ascetic experience of hardship. Everything else is machine work and our accommodations and their infrastructure are going to be pre-installed by machines--robot outposts or telebases. So projects like HI-SEAS are simulating the entirely wrong thing and creating a false impression of life in space attractive to no one but a few space cadets. They're based on an increasingly anachronistic idea of how we will do things in space. Maybe we'll see one or two flag planting missions to Mars in this century. They'll do some good science--at the worst possible ROI--and won't amount to anything in the context of actual settlement.

We should be thinking about what it means to live well in space, not camp there, leveraging the technology we know is emergent on making that accessible. We need to be thinking about models of The Good Life out there because there's now no other practical reason for going there. It's a lifestyle choice. That's it. If we can't make that compelling and attractive then it's just the machines. There aren't going to be paying jobs out there.

And what's interesting about that context is that it doesn't need space agency facilities to explore because it's not really rocket science, it's interior design and gardening. You see, we already know what the basic architecture everywhere we want to setup shop in space is likely to be; big, large span, mostly windowless, functionally generic spaces outfit by retrofit. Domes, vaults, spheres, and cylinders. These may be assembled from parts, built up like concrete shells, excavated out of the living rock, or eventually even grown like organisms. They may have different particulars about their engineering and construction. Different approaches to energy and life support. Different locations will have different logistics strategies. Those technical details don't really matter that much because they'll all be pre-built by machines and largely the same thing on the inside. Everything inside is retrofit and largely independent of the host enclosure. And so the real challenge of living in space is figuring out how to live comfortably and well, using a certain spectrum of materials from ISRU and certain light industry, when you're indoors almost perpetually. That question doesn't need rocket science to explore. It just needs imagination and the skills of the average Maker. We can do that exploration anywhere we can find analogous disused spaces. Places like the Kansas City Subtropolis. Aircraft and airship hangars. Hi-SEAS was based on an off-the-shelf tent-dome made by Pacific Domes, a modded shipping container, and an interior mezannine made by a local architect all assembled by a bunch of vollunteers. It something that could have been done at a Maker Faire.
